title: Hurricane Polo surf is best watched from the sand
dek: Hurricane Polo sent big swells to Southern California beaches this week, and the safest way to admire the surf is from a distance.
body: Hurricane Polo stayed far off the coast of Mexico, and its swell still reached Southern California. Forecasters said south-facing beaches in Southern California could see surf of 4 to 7 feet on Monday and Tuesday, and a coastal flood advisory ran until 5 p.m. today for beaches in Ventura and Los Angeles counties.

One detail stands out. Forecasters noted that the surf would be smaller than it was during Hurricane Marie, and that the erosion left behind from that storm could make flooding worse. The beach has not had much time to recover, and neither have some of the people who live right along it.

The National Weather Service asked people to stay out of the water because of dangerous rip currents, to keep off the rock jetties, and to protect property in flood-prone spots. Those are simple requests, and they are easy to ignore when the waves look beautiful and the evening is warm.

The pull is easy to understand. Big surf is exciting to see, and a storm you cannot feel on land seems harmless. The ocean does not work that way, and the lifeguards and first responders who go in after people have enough to do this week.
If you head to the coast tomorrow to see what the swell left behind, enjoy it from the sand and give the jetties and the water a pass until the surf settles down.
